1: This is the technical deep dive for Book 02 of the Federal Modernization Workbook, Identity and Directory.
It's for the architects and engineers who will actually run the move from Active Directory to Microsoft Entra ID.
Part 1 is assessing the forest: first what an ordinary account can learn without any elevated access, then the full privileged assessment and the evidence trail behind it.
Part 2 is building the Entra ID target and moving onto it: the big design decisions, governance, the eleven-phase playbook, and a reference deployment that runs the whole sequence on one estate.
The slides carry the tables and decision matrices, and the code lives in the chapters and appendices.
2: Federal policy moved the access decision off the network and onto identity.
O M B M twenty-two oh-nine, nist's zero trust architecture and sis-uh's maturity model all point the same way: no trust from network location, and phishing-resistant sign-in.
That makes the identity provider the policy decision point for the whole estate.
Whatever it believes about a person, a group or a device gets enforced everywhere.
Microsoft isn't retiring Active Directory, but its investment is clearly moving to the cloud, from the sync engine to sign-in to the deprecation of N T L M.
The trap is the lift and shift.
Sync the forest as it stands, and the stale accounts and undocumented trusts come with it, while the intent the organizational unit (O U) tree carried has nowhere to land.
3: So what actually has to move?
Two points drive everything in this session.
In Active Directory, where an object sits in the O U tree decides who manages it and which policy applies.
It governs objects by what they carry: attributes, memberships and roles.
Administrative units help, but they can't nest, and for synced users the attribute values are still written on-premises.
Second, the surface is bigger than users and groups.
The program's inventory names eleven dependency types, and some, like P K I, radius and el-dap-bound applications, fail silently when A D goes away.
Each dependency gets an adapter, and the sync engine finishes last.
The rest of this session is how you find all of that, rebuild it, and prove it.
4: An assessment team rarely gets privileged access on day one, so the program spends that waiting time learning what the directory already tells every employee.
It changes nothing, and it turns the request for elevated access into a list built from evidence.
5: It's surprising how much an ordinary domain account can read.
The O U tree and its Group Policy links, which is the structure the attribute design will replace.
Users, groups, computers and service principal names, which is your identity inventory.
What you usually can't see is replication health and D N S server settings; those become a delegation item.
The default is broad because of a handful of built-in read grants, and exactly how broad depends on choices made when the domain was created.
So the first step is a pre-flight that tests what this account can really read in this forest, and every later export records which access it relied on.
6: The assessment report should never claim coverage it doesn't have, so you need to know exactly where that read boundary sits.
Protected accounts: the admin count flag marks accounts that are or were privileged, which makes it a good clean-up list, but not the current privileged population.
Confidential attributes, like LAPS passwords: you can't read them, but the presence and age of the expiration attribute still shows coverage.
Password secrets, which leave a domain controller only through replication rights the assessment never asks for, though who already holds those rights is a key later check.
And restricted containers like Deleted Objects.
The rule that ties it together is simple: report only what you actually measured.
7: Every gap that read-only discovery couldn't close gets written down: what's missing, the narrowest right or export that closes it, why the plan needs it, and whether there's a read-only substitute.
Some come as exports from the right administrator, like replication health or the CA's issued-certificate database.
Some, like LAPS and BitLocker recovery data, are never requested at all.
The gap list becomes a short written request with firm rules: read only, specific to an object and a reason, time-bound, one named account, and an export wherever possible.
Domain Admin for the assessment is not an acceptable line.
Tell security operations first, because broad directory queries look like reconnaissance, and keep the output encrypted, because it's a map of the estate.
8: Module 2 is the full assessment of the forest.
Chapter 08 fills the gap list with the privileged half of discovery.
The program's position is that the assessment produces evidence, not just script output: fixed artifacts, a hashed manifest, and every run committed to Git.
9: The full assessment covers eight areas in a fixed order, from forest topology through to trusts.
Most of the forest is readable by any authenticated user, so each collector runs on the narrowest right that works, like read on the O U security descriptors, or read on the P K I containers.
Two rights the source design asked for are refused.
DnsAdmins membership, because Microsoft treats it as privileged.
And standing Domain Admin, because no run needs it.
Trust verification is the only step that does, and it runs separately under just-in-time elevation.
Collection runs from a domain-joined Windows Server 2025 or Windows 11 host, under a group managed service account, so no password is ever stored.
Next, the three areas that carry most of the planning weight.
10: Three areas carry most of the planning weight.
Record every operations master role, and remember there are three per domain plus two for the forest, so a three-domain forest has eleven to record, not five.
Flag any functional level below Windows Server 2016, because it blocks the domain controller refresh.
The goal is to capture what it encodes, so the attribute design reproduces intent, not structure.
The delegations someone made by hand become the administrative unit candidates.
Third, Group Policy, the biggest artifact.
Every live setting moves to Intune, moves elsewhere, or retires, and overlapping settings have to be resolved first, because Intune's migration refuses conflicting values.
11: A D CS matters twice in a migration.
It issues the certificates devices, domain controllers and smart cards rely on, and its misconfigurations are among the most direct paths to privilege escalation in a forest.
The assessment checks the known patterns it can see, the ESC family from SpecterOps' 2021 research, with Defender for Identity's definitions as the reference.
The correction that matters most: the source's ESC1 check looked for a key usage almost every template has, so it flagged nearly everything.
The real test is whether the template allows an authentication purpose, and a template only counts if a CA actually publishes it and broad groups can enroll.
Fixing it belongs to the P K I owner, through Book 07.
12: Every computer object is a migration decision: Entra join, hybrid join, Azure Arc, retire, or keep in Active Directory.
Delegation is where the source got things wrong, so classify by what's actually set.
Unconstrained delegation lets a service impersonate any user to any service.
Domain controllers are expected to have it; anywhere else, it's a critical issue.
Treat a computer as stale only when both its last logon and its password are old, because the logon date can lag by up to two weeks.
For users, expand the privileged groups recursively, so nested members aren't missed.
And among service accounts, user accounts with service principal names are Kerberoastable, which makes them the highest priority to replace.
13: Trusts are where undocumented history usually hides.
The trust attributes are bit flags, so decode them from the published specification, not from memory, and keep the raw value too, so bits added later aren't lost.
Then state direction plainly, because it's easy to get backwards: access flows the opposite way to trust.
The source design had it reversed.
So for each trust, the assessment says in plain words which side's users can reach which side's resources.
Selective authentication and SID filtering are posture, not findings.
Verification needs administrative credentials, so it runs as its own elevated step.
And a forest trust doesn't convert into anything in Entra ID.
It marks a partner whose access has to be redesigned, which Module 4 covers.
14: What makes a run evidence is the pipeline around the collectors.
Every run writes a manifest with a SHA-256 hash of every output file, and a failed step is recorded rather than stopping the run, so a partial run is visible as partial.
Anyone holding the repository can recompute the hashes and show nothing changed after collection.
Each run becomes a single commit on its own branch, not hundreds of commits.
Issues are raised automatically for only two classes, critical P K I patterns and unconstrained delegation outside the domain controllers; everything else feeds the planning documents.
Run it weekly, and compare objects by a stable key, not timestamps, to see what drifted.
And handle the data carefully, because it's a map for an attacker.
15: Part 2 builds the Entra ID target and migrates onto it, starting with Module 3, the target design.
The premise fits in one sentence: in Active Directory, where an object sits decides what applies to it; in Entra ID, what an object says about itself decides.
16: Before any object moves, break the A D model into its parts, because each lands somewhere different.
O U's do three jobs: policy scoping becomes Conditional Access and Intune profiles, delegation becomes administrative units, and organization becomes dynamic groups and attributes.
The forest becomes the tenant, trusts become cross-tenant access, and AdminSDHolder's purpose is served by Privileged Identity Management and protected actions.
The design principle is that Entra ID inverts the model.
Attributes decide memberships, and memberships decide policy, which is why attribute quality gates everything after it.
Licensing gates the governance features, and the slide has the map.
One date to act on: the preview member-of operator ends November 3, 2026, so replace any rules that use it now.
17: The first hybrid-period decision is the sync engine.
Connect Sync is the long-standing, full-featured engine on a Windows Server.
Cloud Sync is a lightweight agent configured from the cloud, and Microsoft now calls it the strategic direction.
The slide compares them side by side.
The short version: Cloud Sync runs multiple active agents with automatic failover, while Connect Sync still wins on scale and advanced rules.
Cloud Sync now covers group provisioning back to A D and Exchange hybrid writeback, so those no longer force Connect.
The program's rule is Cloud Sync for new deployments, and Connect only where a forest needs something Cloud Sync can't do.
Both can run in one forest with separate scopes, so you can move in stages.
18: The second decision is where passwords are checked.
With password hash sync, it happens in the cloud, needs no extra infrastructure, and survives an on-premises outage.
Pass-through authentication depends on on-premises agents, and federation with A D FS needs whole server farms.

Microsoft recommends turning on password hash sync whichever method you choose, because it's the fallback, and organizations that had it on recovered from ransomware outages in hours rather than weeks.
So the program prefers it everywhere, and A D FS becomes a decommission target.
When sync meets an object that already exists in the cloud, a match overwrites the cloud copy, so clean A D first.
And since July 1, 2026, sync can't hard-match onto cloud accounts with privileged roles, so don't plan to take over admins that way.
19: Groups and service accounts each get one recorded decision per object.
Entra ID has no group scope, so the classic A D nesting model doesn't map one to one.
Every security group gets one of five outcomes: keep it in A D, sync it, convert it to cloud-only, make it dynamic, or retire it.
Nesting also works for fewer things in Entra ID, since app assignment and licensing don't cascade, so flatten deep chains and record the mapping.
For service accounts, the rule is to eliminate stored secrets.

Accounts that call cloud APIs become app registrations with certificates or federated credentials, Azure workloads get managed identities, and on-premises Kerberos workloads go to group managed service accounts.
Every app gets two human owners, and no client secrets in production.
20: Privileged access has one core rule: no standing access.
Every privileged assignment is eligible and activated just in time, and the only permanent ones are the two emergency accounts.
Domain Admins maps to Global Administrator, held by very few, and most of its duties map to narrower roles.
The slide has the full mapping, which is the program's design, not an exact equivalence.
Activation is short, four hours at most for the top roles, with approval and a ticket, and it forces a fresh phishing-resistant sign-in.
Name approvers outside the requester's chain, because with none configured, pim can lock the tenant.
The emergency accounts are cloud-only, excluded from restrictive policies, alerted on every sign-in, and tested at least every ninety days.
21: Conditional Access replaces the logon restrictions and network controls A D enforced through Group Policy.
The program organizes it around personas, populations with different needs and risks: internal staff, admins, partners, guests, service accounts, and the break-glass group.
One tip: target admins by group, because role targeting doesn't cover scoped or custom roles.
The baseline set, CA001 through CA017, runs from blocking legacy sign-in for everyone to requiring phishing-resistant strength for admins.
Book 04's library is the authoritative set and extends it for the sis-uh baseline.
Rollout is staged: report-only, then a pilot, then phased waves, each behind a monitoring gate.
And never switch an all-users policy straight from off to on without confirming both emergency accounts still sign in.
22: Module 4 is migrating, governing and proving it.
Chapter 10 states the finish line: the migration ends when governance runs on its own.
Joiners, movers and leavers flow from HR without a ticket, and drift shows up in a diff instead of an incident.
23: Governance in Active Directory was mostly a ticket queue: someone asked for access, someone added it, and nobody took it away.
The target replaces that with a loop.

HR-driven provisioning creates the account, Lifecycle Workflows run the joiner, mover and leaver tasks, access packages grant access with an expiry, and access reviews remove what's no longer justified.
For example, seven days before the hire date the manager is emailed a Temporary Access Pass, so the new hire registers a phishing-resistant credential on day one.
On the leave date, the account is disabled and its sessions revoked.
Two cautions: remove privileged access before the delete task runs, and delete synced users in A D, or they come back on the next sync.
24: Authentication modernization starts from the federal requirement.
O M B M twenty-two oh-nine requires phishing-resistant M F A, and an end to methods like SMS and voice codes for routine access.
Its targets were set for the end of fiscal year 2024, so these are requirements now, not goals.
Older plans put smart cards last, but a federal workforce already carries piv or CAC cards, so certificate-based authentication straight against Entra ID is the fastest path.
The program goes in four phases: privileged accounts first, then every card holder, then managed Windows devices on Windows Hello, then everyone else on passkeys.
Then the legacy cutoff: find the remaining legacy sign-ins, move them, block them, and watch for thirty days until there are none.
25: The migration runs in eleven phases, zero through ten, and each one starts only when the previous one's validation criteria are met.
Every phase also has a rollback procedure.
The durations are planning estimates, not measured results, and the total runs forty to seventy weeks.
It starts with the assessment, then the sync deployment, with object counts matching within one percent.
Then sign-in, groups, service accounts and pim, which ends with no permanent admin assignments except the emergency accounts.
Conditional Access is enforced only after M F A registration passes ninety-five percent in each population.
Then come the phishing-resistant roadmap, the legacy cutoff, retiring federation, and finally steady-state governance, with the operations runbook committed to Git.
26: Proving it starts with logs, because Entra ID keeps them only briefly: seven days on the free tier, thirty on P1 or P2, and upgrading doesn't recover older data.
So stream everything to Log Analytics and keep sign-in and audit logs for three hundred sixty-five days.
On top of that, scheduled detections watch for things like stale accounts, late-night privileged activations, and any emergency account sign-in.
For compliance, the controls map to fed-ramp twenty X Key Security Indicators, evidenced by the workflows, reviews and pim you've already built.
A weekly scan compares against a baseline and opens an issue with the diff, and each finding is fixed at the source, never by editing the copy.
Today that covers user additions and removals; the rest is planned.
27: Chapter 11 puts it all together on one representative estate.
It's a composite, not a real engagement, and the counts are illustrative.
Picture about fifty thousand users in two forests, joined by a forest trust nobody documented or owns, moving to Microsoft 365 G C C.
There are five phases, and each ends with a signed readiness bundle that the next one starts from.

Discovery finds about four hundred accounts with service principal names, and every SQL Server one is captured, because a missing one silently falls back to N T L M. Normalizing resolves a clash between two Operations O U's in an organizational registry, not by renaming groups.
Mapping finds four adapters that carry the risk, including P K I and radius, which move in lockstep.
Then migration and validation, with every operation recorded.
28: During migration, the program classifies drift into five kinds, and it's honest about maturity: two are detected automatically today, one partly, and two still rely on people reviewing the assessment.
From Phase 2 on, the agency can produce an evidence bundle at any time, with the readiness bundles, the SPN inventories, the provenance chain and every drift finding.
It goes to the security control assessor and the authorizing official as the work happens, not assembled over most of a year afterward.
And it belongs to the agency.
When the integrator leaves, the evidence stays.
So, from Monday: start read-only discovery, keep the access request narrow, make every run evidence, and gate every phase.
